After removing 30 percent of the edges at random (here B–D, C–D, and D–E, drawn dashed), every node survives but the graph has split into the triangle A, B, C and the four nodes D, E, F, G." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with a fraction of edges removed uniformly at random. All nodes are preserved. This is the basic operation of *bond percolation* and models random link failures: cables cut, roads closed, friendships lapsing, or interactions that fail to transmit an infection. Comparing the surviving graph with the original (for example, with `largest_component_size()`) shows how dependent the network's connectivity is on individual links. Typical uses include: - stress-testing communication or transport networks against random link failures - simulating an epidemic in which each contact transmits only with some probability - generating perturbed versions of a graph for sensitivity analyses The number of edges removed is `round(q * m)`, where `m` is the edge count, so the removed fraction is exact up to rounding, and every edge is equally likely to be chosen. Because nodes are never removed, a node can end up isolated. To remove nodes instead, use `node_percolation()`. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the directedness of the original, and nodes and surviving edges keep their IDs, labels, weights and attributes. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [q]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fraction of edges to remove, between `0.0` and `1.0` inclusive. For example, `q=0.2` removes 20% of the edges. `q=0.0` keeps every edge and `q=1.0` leaves only the isolated nodes. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed for the random number generator. Calls with the same graph, `q=`, and `seed=` remove the same edges, which makes results reproducible. If `None` (default), a fresh random seed is drawn on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph containing all of the original nodes but only the surviving edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `q=` is outside the range `[0.0, 1.0]`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below has ten edges: two clusters (A, B, C and E, F, G) joined through the hub D. Removing 30% of the edges deletes three of them. With this seed the three lost edges are exactly the links B-D, C-D, and D-E, so all seven nodes survive but the largest connected piece now holds only four of them: ::: {#8c3427d9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("E", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G")]) ) percolated = graph.edge_percolation(q=0.3, seed=14) (percolated.count_nodes(), percolated.count_edges(), percolated.largest_component_size()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (7, 7, 4) ``` ::: ::: Node IDs and labels carry over unchanged, so the surviving edges can be listed by label to see exactly which links were kept: ::: {#3f56db2a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = percolated.get_edge_df() sorted( "-".join(sorted([percolated.get_label_from_id(s), percolated.get_label_from_id(t)])) for s, t in zip(edges["source"], edges["target"]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A-B', 'A-C', 'B-C', 'D-F', 'E-F', 'E-G', 'F-G'] ``` ::: :::
